opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Sarah. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group that studies how people see changes at work, and nothing you tell me will be linked to your name.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I use this stuff every day, so I've got opinions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool. It already does half my takeoffs, which is counting up materials from the drawings, and most of my schedules. So I spend more time on the interesting parts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even in the calm version, half my job is software. That's fine as long as the other half grows. I'd want to move toward project management, where it's more about people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get my project management certificate. Keep paying down the loan. Ask to run a small job myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, mostly. It's the world I'm already in.

S0.say: It's a useful tool. It does half my takeoffs and schedules, so I get the interesting parts.
S0.think: Half my job is already software. That's fine as long as the other half grows.
S0.do: Works toward a project management certificate, pays down her loan and asks to run a small job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's how it's already playing out. Firms are hiring fewer grads and expecting juniors to do more with the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm a junior, so fewer beginners hits close. I'm in, but stepping up gets harder when there are fewer people below you. I'd need to get out of pure estimating.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Push to get on site more. Learn the parts of the job that are about people and the physical build, not spreadsheets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'd want to move before the ground does.

S1.say: That's already happening. Firms hire fewer grads and expect juniors to do more with the tools.
S1.think: Fewer beginners hits close. I need to get out of pure estimating.
S1.do: Pushes to spend more time on site, learning the people and building side of the job.
S1.feel: Uneasy. Wants to move before the ground does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who learn to direct AI will be fine, and the ones who don't will struggle. Bit harsh, but it's what I see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Estimating and scheduling is exactly the routine desk work in this picture. I'm good, but the agent doesn't need to be good. Just good enough and cheap. And I've still got student debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Apply for site engineer roles right away. Build up three months of savings. Maybe do estimating for small builders on the side, using the same tools that are replacing me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like a clock is running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your public line is that people who learn the tools will be fine. You know the tools well. Do you feel fine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Which tells you how much I believe my own line.

S2.say: The people who learn to direct AI will be fine. The ones who don't will struggle.
S2.think: Estimating is exactly the routine desk work here. The agent only needs to be good enough and cheap.
S2.do: Applies for site engineer roles, builds three months of savings and starts estimating for small builders on the side.
S2.feel: Anxious, like a clock is running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the gains have to be shared somehow, and that graduates were sold a promise that's now broken.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job's gone in this one. Project engineering is thinking work. All that's left is the site, the physical side. And I'm still paying for a degree for a career that just disappeared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get a site role, even a step down in title, because physical work is safe here. Honestly, look at a trade, like an electrician's apprenticeship. Ask about pausing my loan payments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. And angry about the debt.

S3.say: The gains have to be shared, and graduates were sold a promise that's now broken.
S3.think: My job's gone. I'm still paying for a degree for a career that just disappeared.
S3.do: Takes a site role even at a lower title, looks into an electrician's apprenticeship and asks to pause her loan payments.
S3.feel: Alarmed, and angry about the debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a proper plan. Retraining, income support, all of it. Not just 'learn to code' or 'learn a trade'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now even the site isn't safe. The backup I had in the last one is gone. My only edge is that I know both the software and the site, so maybe I can be the person who plans the robot work. That's a narrow door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Go after any role coordinating robots on building sites. Talk to the robot companies directly. Get a flatmate to cut my rent. Keep the loan on the minimum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still alarmed. And tired of planning backups.

S4.say: We need a proper plan: retraining and income support, not just 'learn a trade'.
S4.think: Even the site isn't safe now. Knowing both software and site might let me plan the robot work, but that's a narrow door.
S4.do: Goes after roles coordinating robots on sites, contacts robot companies, gets a flatmate and keeps her loan on the minimum.
S4.feel: Alarmed, and tired of planning backups.
